light.notes: Your sunniest window. Move it outside gradually in summer, or it sunburns brown.

water.notes: Soak the compost, then let it dry out completely before watering again.

soil.notes: Gritty cactus mix in a pot with a drainage hole; terracotta is ideal.

toxicity.notes: Contains saponins and anthraquinones. Eating it causes vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy in pets. The yellow latex just under the skin is a strong laxative for people.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed two or three times in spring and summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years, into a wide, shallow pot; it gets top-heavy.
guides.pruning: Cut damaged or outer leaves off at the base.
guides.propagation: Remove offsets (pups) with roots, let them dry for a day, then pot up.

problems.fix: Stop watering until the compost is completely dry, and check the base for rot.
Soak the compost thoroughly.
Move it to the sunniest window you have.

guides.growthHabit: Rosette of thick, spiky-edged, gel-filled leaves; forms clumps of pups.

light.notes: Lots of light, including direct sun. Leaf edges turn red in strong sun.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out completely, then water thoroughly.

soil.notes: Gritty, fast-draining mix in a heavy pot to stop it tipping.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs. Eating it can cause vomiting, lethargy and wobbliness.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed two or three times in spring and summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2–4 years. It likes being snug.
guides.pruning: Prune in spring to shape it into a tree; cut just above a pair of leaves.
guides.propagation: Stem or single-leaf cuttings, dried for a few days and laid on gritty compost.

problems.cause: Thirst — or rotten roots that can't take up water
problems.fix: If the compost is dry, water. If it's wet, check the roots for rot.

problems.cause: Overwatering or a sudden cold spell
problems.fix: Let it dry out and keep it above 7°C.

problems.symptom: Leggy stems with gaps between leaves
problems.fix: Move it into direct sun and prune back.

guides.growthHabit: Branching, tree-like succulent with thick stems and glossy oval leaves.

light.notes: Full sun keeps the rosette tight and colourful.

water.notes: Soak and dry: water thoroughly, then wait until the compost is completely dry. Keep water out of the rosette.

soil.notes: Gritty cactus mix with extra grit or pumice.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.
guides.propagation: Offsets, or leaves twisted cleanly off and laid on dry grit.

problems.fix: Move it into full sun; behead and re-root badly stretched plants.
Stop watering and remove affected leaves.

guides.growthHabit: Tight, blue-grey rosettes that form clumps.

light.notes: Full sun for a compact, powdery rosette.

water.notes: Soak and dry. Water the compost, not the rosette.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.

problems.fix: Give it full sun.
Repot in dry grit and water far less.

guides.growthHabit: Pale silver-blue rosettes that spread by offsets.

light.notes: Bright light with little direct sun. Unlike most succulents it scorches in hot sun, turning red-brown.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out completely, then water thoroughly.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years, into a wide, shallow pot.

problems.fix: Move it out of hot, direct light.
Stop watering until completely dry.

guides.growthHabit: Small rosettes of dark leaves banded with white bumps; forms clumps.

light.notes: Bright light without hot direct sun.

water.notes: Soak and dry.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.

problems.fix: Shade from hot sun; water when fully dry.
Repot in dry grit.

light.notes: Bright light with some direct sun.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out, then water thoroughly.

soil.notes: Gritty, fast-draining mix in a hanging pot.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.
guides.repotting: Rarely — the leaves fall off at a touch. Only when essential.
guides.propagation: Fallen leaves root readily on dry grit.

problems.fix: Hang it where it won't be brushed, and let it dry between waterings.
Water thoroughly.

guides.growthHabit: Trailing stems densely covered in plump, blue-green leaves.

light.notes: Bright light with a little gentle direct sun.

water.notes: Water when the top couple of centimetres are dry. The pearls flatten slightly when thirsty.

soil.notes: Gritty mix in a shallow pot; the roots are shallow.

toxicity.notes: Generally considered mildly toxic. Eating it can cause vomiting and diarrhoea, and the sap can irritate skin.

guides.feeding: Half-strength cactus feed monthly in spring and summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2 years; keep the crown level with the compost.
guides.propagation: Lay strand cuttings on damp grit; they root where the pearls touch.

problems.fix: Water, and shade from hot afternoon sun.
Let it dry out; restart from healthy strands if the top has rotted.

light.notes: Bright light with some direct sun. It needs long nights to flower again.

water.notes: Let the top half of the compost dry, then water thoroughly.

toxicity.notes: Contains bufadienolides (heart-affecting compounds). Eating it causes vomiting and diarrhoea; heart rhythm problems are rare.

guides.pruning: Cut spent flower stalks back to the leaves.
guides.propagation: Stem cuttings, dried for a day before potting.

problems.fix: From autumn, give it 14 hours of complete darkness each night for about six weeks.
Let it dry out more between waterings.

guides.growthHabit: Compact, with glossy scalloped leaves and dense clusters of small flowers.

light.notes: Bright light with some direct sun keeps the brown tips vivid.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out completely. Water the compost, not the furry leaves.

toxicity.notes: Like other Kalanchoe it contains bufadienolides. Eating it causes vomiting and diarrhoea; heart rhythm problems are rare.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.

problems.fix: Move it into brighter light and cut back.
Stop watering until dry.

guides.growthHabit: Upright, with velvety silver leaves tipped in rust-brown.

light.notes: Bright, indirect light. It's a forest cactus: hot direct sun turns it red and limp.

water.notes: Unlike desert cacti, water when the top 2–3cm is dry — never let it dry out completely.
water.restingSeason: Every 2 weeks; a little less after flowering.

soil.notes: Light, free-draining mix: compost with bark and perlite.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed monthly from spring until late summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years after flowering. It flowers best a little pot-bound.
guides.propagation: Twist off a section of two or three segments and push it into damp compost.

problems.cause: Being moved, a draught, or a swing in temperature
problems.fix: Once buds form, leave it in the same place and water consistently.

problems.cause: Too warm, or too much light in the evening
problems.fix: In autumn give it cool nights (10–15°C) and long, uninterrupted darkness.
Water if dry; if the compost is wet, check for rot.

guides.growthHabit: Arching, segmented stems with bright flowers at the tips.

light.notes: Full sun.

water.notes: Soak, then let it dry out completely.
water.restingSeason: Barely at all; a cool, dry winter helps it flower.

guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years, wearing thick gloves or wrapping it in folded newspaper.
guides.propagation: Detach a pad, let it dry for a few days, then set it upright on grit.

problems.fix: Let it dry out and water far less.
Move it into full sun.

guides.growthHabit: Flat pads covered in dots of tiny barbed bristles (glochids) that lodge in skin at a touch.

light.notes: Full sun for flowers all year.

water.notes: Let the top half of the compost dry out.
water.restingSeason: Every 3–4 weeks. It may drop leaves if kept too dry and cold.

toxicity.notes: The milky sap is a strong irritant: it burns skin and eyes, and eating the plant causes mouth irritation and vomiting. Wear gloves and eye protection when pruning.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed monthly in spring and summer.
guides.pruning: Prune in spring, wearing gloves. Dip cuts in cold water to stop the sap.
guides.propagation: Tip cuttings, dried for a few days before potting.

problems.fix: Keep it above 10°C and water when the top half is dry.
Give it the sunniest spot you have.

guides.growthHabit: Spiny, sprawling stems with small leaves and red, pink or yellow flower bracts.

light.notes: Bright light with some direct sun.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out, then water thoroughly.

soil.notes: Gritty mix in a heavy pot; it becomes top-heavy.

toxicity.notes: Despite looking like a cactus, it's a euphorbia: the milky sap burns skin and eyes and is harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling cut stems.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed monthly in spring and summer.
guides.propagation: Stem cuttings, with the sap rinsed off and the cut left to dry for a week.

problems.fix: Use a heavier pot, stake it, and turn it regularly.
Cut above the rot and let the healthy piece callus.

guides.growthHabit: Upright, branching, ribbed stems with small leaves along the edges.

light.notes: Full sun.

water.notes: Soak, then let the compost dry out.

guides.feeding: Cactus feed once or twice in summer.
guides.pruning: Takes hard pruning well; popular for bonsai.

problems.fix: Let it dry out and give it more sun.
Water thoroughly.

guides.growthHabit: Shrubby, with reddish stems and small round leaves. Often confused with jade plant, which it isn't.

light.notes: Full sun.

water.notes: Let the soil dry out completely.
water.restingSeason: Almost none; keep dry and frost-free in winter.

toxicity.notes: The sap irritates skin and can cause a rash. Leaf tips are needle-sharp — place it away from paths, children and pets.

problems.fix: Keep it dry in winter and grow it in gritty soil.
Move it into full sun.

guides.growthHabit: Large rosette of thick, spine-tipped grey leaves. Flowers once after many years, then the rosette dies.

light.notes: Full sun for the darkest colour; light shade in the hottest weather.

water.notes: Aeoniums grow in the cool months and rest in summer heat — the reverse of most succulents.
water.growingSeason: Water sparingly: the rosettes close up and rest in summer heat.
water.restingSeason: This is when it grows. Water when the top of the soil is dry, and keep it frost-free.

guides.feeding: Half-strength feed monthly while it's actively growing.
guides.propagation: Cut a rosette with some stem, let it dry for a few days, then pot it.

problems.symptom: Rosettes closing up and dropping leaves in summer
problems.fix: Water less and give it light shade until it cools down.
Keep it much drier in summer.

guides.growthHabit: Branching stems topped with flat rosettes.

light.notes: Tolerates shade but grows best in bright light with some sun.

water.notes: Let the compost dry out completely.

toxicity.notes: Like other snake plants it contains saponins. Chewing can cause drooling, vomiting and diarrhoea.

guides.feeding: Two or three times in spring and summer at most.

problems.fix: Stop watering and repot into dry, gritty mix if rotting.
Move it somewhere brighter.

guides.growthHabit: Stiff, round, spear-like leaves, often sold braided.

light.notes: Full sun outdoors. It doesn't do well as a houseplant.

water.notes: Rain is usually enough in the ground. In pots, water only when bone dry.
water.restingSeason: None in pots; keep them out of standing winter wet.

soil.notes: Poor, gritty, very free-draining soil; ideal in gravel, walls and troughs.

guides.repotting: Divide crowded clumps every few years.
guides.propagation: Detach the 'chicks' and press them into gritty soil.

problems.cause: Each rosette flowers once, then dies
problems.fix: Normal — remove it; the offsets around it carry on.
Improve drainage with grit and avoid saucers.

guides.growthHabit: Low, tight rosettes that spread by offsets into mats.

toxicity.notes: Aloes contain saponins and anthraquinones that cause vomiting and diarrhoea if eaten.
